reference.source: Standard vascular surgery reference texts and peripheral arterial disease consensus guidance
clinicalPearls: A form of severe aortoiliac occlusive disease described by a classic triad of bilateral buttock, hip and thigh claudication, erectile dysfunction (impotence) in men, and absent or diminished femoral pulses
Results from atherosclerotic occlusion at the aortic bifurcation and iliac arteries, reducing inflow to both lower limbs
Typically affects patients with major atherosclerotic risk factors, particularly smoking, and often at a relatively younger age than distal disease
Claudication is proximal (buttock and thigh) rather than calf-predominant because the flow limitation is high in the arterial tree
Chronic collateralisation may mean the limbs are viable at rest despite extensive occlusion, so critical ischaemia is not always present
The ankle-brachial index is reduced and cross-sectional angiography defines the extent of aortoiliac disease
Management combines cardiovascular risk reduction and supervised exercise with revascularisation (endovascular stenting or aortobifemoral bypass) for lifestyle-limiting or critical disease
reference.pathophysiology: Leriche syndrome is caused by progressive atherosclerotic narrowing and occlusion of the distal abdominal aorta and both common iliac arteries at the aortic bifurcation. The resulting reduction in inflow to the pelvis and lower limbs produces exercise-induced ischaemia of the gluteal and thigh muscles, causing proximal claudication, and impaired penile arterial supply, causing erectile dysfunction. Because the disease develops gradually, collateral pathways enlarge to maintain resting perfusion, which explains why the limbs are often viable despite absent femoral pulses; when demand exceeds this collateral supply, symptoms and, in advanced disease, tissue loss occur.
additionalDifferentials: Femoropopliteal or infrainguinal peripheral arterial disease
Spinal (neurogenic) claudication from lumbar canal stenosis
Hip or lumbar degenerative joint disease
Chronic venous disease with venous claudication
Aortic dissection or coarctation affecting distal flow
additionalInvestigations: Ankle-brachial pressure index and segmental limb pressures to quantify inflow disease
Duplex ultrasound of the aortoiliac and femoral segments
CT or MR angiography to map the extent of aortoiliac occlusion and plan intervention
Catheter angiography when endovascular treatment is planned
Assessment of cardiovascular risk factors and coexisting coronary and carotid disease
Exercise testing where the diagnosis of claudication is uncertain
redFlags: Rest pain, ulceration or gangrene indicating critical limb-threatening ischaemia
Acute limb ischaemia from superimposed thrombosis or embolism
Rapidly progressive symptoms or tissue loss
Widespread atherosclerosis heralding high coronary and cerebrovascular event risk
reference.prognosis: Revascularisation, particularly aortobifemoral bypass, has durable long-term patency and reliably relieves claudication and often erectile dysfunction; however, the underlying atherosclerosis means overall prognosis is dominated by cardiovascular risk, so aggressive risk-factor management is essential.
pitfalls: Attributing buttock and thigh symptoms to spinal or hip disease and missing aortoiliac occlusion
Failing to palpate or document femoral pulses in a patient with claudication
Overlooking erectile dysfunction as a vascular symptom of the syndrome
Neglecting systemic cardiovascular risk reduction while focusing only on the limbs
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
Global vascular guidelines on peripheral arterial disease management
